Syria
sĭr'ĭ-ă
n. (the Aramean country north-east of Israel, capital Damascus — Israel's nearest and most persistent rival, and the province where believers were first called Christians)
The KJV renders Hebrew 'Aram as Syria, following the Greek Syria, which is probably a shortening of Assyria though the two are distinct. Aram is a son of Shem (Gen 10:22), and Aramaic is the language of the region — the tongue of parts of Daniel and Ezra and the common speech of Judea in our Lord's day.

Biblical Definition

Syria is Aram, the highland country reaching from the Lebanon range north and east to the Euphrates, and Damascus was its heart. Its relations with Israel run the whole scale. David subdued it — “then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus: and the Syrians became servants to David” (2Sa 8:6). Under the divided monarchy it became the standing threat, and the Elisha narratives are largely Syrian: the raiding bands, Naaman's leprosy, the blinded army led into Samaria and fed, the siege lifted by a sound of chariots no one else heard. Isaiah's ministry turns on a Syrian alliance: “Syria is confederate with Ephraim” (Isa 7:2), and Ahaz's terror at it produced the promise of Immanuel. In the New Testament Syria is a Roman province: the census that brought Joseph to Bethlehem was taken “when Cyrenius was governor of Syria” (Luk 2:2), our Lord's fame “went throughout all Syria” (Mat 4:24), and Saul was on the Damascus road when he was struck down. Antioch in Syria became the first Gentile church, the place where the disciples were called Christians, and the base from which Paul was sent out.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives Syria as a country of Asia, and Syriac as the language of Syria, a dialect of the Aramean nearly allied to the Chaldee.

expand to see more

SYRIA, n. A country of Asia, lying east of the Mediterranean and north of Palestine, whose chief city is Damascus.

It is called Aram in the Hebrew Scriptures, from Aram the son of Shem.

SYRIAC, n. The language of Syria, a dialect of the Aramean or Chaldee tongue.

The Syrians were long the rivals of Israel, and their kings Benhadad and Hazael are famed in the books of the Kings.

Antioch, the capital of Syria under the Romans, was the place where the disciples were first called Christians.

Key Scripture

2Sa 8:6 — "Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus: and the Syrians became servants to David, and brought gifts. And the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went."

Isa 7:2 — "And it was told the house of David, saying, Syria is confederate with Ephraim. And his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind."

Luk 2:2 — "( And this taxing was first made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria.)"

Mat 4:24 — "And his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments, and those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them."

Modern Corruption

Luk 2:2 is the standard exhibit for an error in the gospels; the objection rests on assuming one governorship and one census where the evidence permits neither assumption.

expand to see more

The census under Cyrenius is presented in most handbooks as a demonstrable historical mistake: Quirinius governed Syria and taxed Judea in AD 6, a decade after Herod's death, so Luke has muddled his dates. Several honest answers are available and any one of them dissolves the objection. Luke's Greek can be read “this taxing was before that made when Cyrenius was governor”, distinguishing an earlier enrolment from the famous one — and Luke himself knows about the AD 6 census, since he names it in Act 5:37. Cyrenius may also have held a command in Syria earlier, under Saturninus or Varus; enrolments were multi-year processes, not single days. What is not available is the assumption behind the confident verdict: that a physician who spent two years gathering testimony in Judea, and who names eight Roman officials and gets the rest right, blundered on the one point his readers could most easily check.

The second and more pastoral matter in Syria is Naaman's leprosy, because the Lord Jesus made it a sermon that nearly got Him killed. “Many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus the prophet; and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian” (Luk 4:27). The congregation at Nazareth was filled with wrath, and the reason is plain: He had said that sovereign mercy goes where it pleases, past the covenant people to a Syrian officer. Election is not a doctrine invented at Dort. It is what emptied a synagogue in Galilee and sent the congregation looking for a cliff.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Aram (H758), Aram, rendered Syria; 'Aramith (H762), in the Syrian tongue; Greek Syria (G4947).

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Aram (H758) — Aram; a son of Shem and the highland country his line settled.

Hebrew 'Aram-Dammeseq — Syria of Damascus; the kingdom David garrisoned (2Sa 8:6).

Hebrew 'Aramith (H762) — in Aramaic, in the Syrian tongue; the language of Dan 2:4 through 7:28.

Greek Syria (G4947) — Syria; the Roman province including Antioch and, for a time, Judea.

Greek Christianos (G5546) — Christian; a name first given at Antioch in Syria (Act 11:26).

Usage

"“The Syrians became servants to David” — the high-water mark of the kingdom."

"“Syria is confederate with Ephraim” — the alarm that produced Immanuel."

"“His fame went throughout all Syria” — the Gentile north hearing first."
